stories.title: Dogs Keep Leaping From This Scottish Bridge. Here's Why.
stories.description: Around 300 dogs have jumped from the same Victorian bridge near Dumbarton, almost always from the same side. A canine psychologist and a bird charity worked out what they are smelling. #unsolvedmysteries #history #scotland
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's hook-watch cohort shows that opening on a scene loses hold (Desert shipwrecks, 68.9%), while a bare number opener carries it (Anglo-Zanzibar War's '9:02 to 9:40'), so this hook leads on the count of 300 before naming the bridge.

factual_claims.text: At least 300 dogs have jumped from Overtoun Bridge near Dumbarton, Scotland, which was completed in June 1895 and stands about 50 feet above rocks.
Reports date back to the 1950s, dogs consistently favour one particular side of the bridge, and approximately 50 deaths are documented.
Scottish Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals investigations into the jumps were inconclusive.
Canine psychologist David Sands proposed residual male mink scent as the cause, and the RSPB found nests of mink, mice and squirrels on the favoured side.
The bridge's tapered parapet obscures the drop from an approaching dog, so a dog following the scent cannot see the fall.

segments.narration: Around 300 dogs have jumped from the same Scottish bridge. Overtoun, near Dumbarton. Completed in 1895. A fifty-foot drop to the rocks below.
Reports go back to the 1950s. Almost always the same side. Almost always the same stretch of wall. Around fifty of the dogs have died.
The Scottish SPCA investigated and came away with nothing conclusive. Which leaves the real question: what can a dog sense on a bridge that we cannot?
Smell. Canine psychologist David Sands found it at the base — mink. The RSPB found mink, mouse and squirrel nests on exactly the favoured side.
Male mink scent overwhelms a dog. And the bridge wall tapers, hiding the drop. So the dog leaps at prey it can smell but never sees.

research.summary: Overtoun Bridge, completed June 1895 near Dumbarton, has seen at least 300 dogs jump since the 1950s with about 50 deaths, overwhelmingly from one side. SSPCA investigations were inconclusive. The leading explanation, from canine psychologist David Sands, is residual male mink scent, supported by RSPB findings of mink, mouse and squirrel nests on the favoured side, combined with a tapered parapet that hides the drop. Narration kept non-graphic for a family audience.

verification.note: Confirmed: completed June 1895, approximately 50 feet (15 m).

stories.title: Faces Kept Appearing In A Spanish Kitchen Floor
stories.description: From 1971 faces surfaced in the concrete floor of one house in Andalusia, drawing hundreds of visitors for thirty years. A chemistry lab and an infrared camera finally explained them. #unsolvedmysteries #history #spain
stories.editorial_rationale: Brief evidence puts a concrete physical impossibility at the top of the hook cohort (Mirage of Constanz, 187.7%) and scene-setting at the bottom (Desert shipwrecks, 68.9%), so this hook states the face in the floor plainly and holds the village and date for line two.

factual_claims.text: The first face appeared in Maria Gomez Camara's kitchen floor at Calle Real 5 in Belmez de la Moraleda, Jaen, Spain, on 23 August 1971.
The family destroyed the first image, a second face then appeared, and the mayor ordered that one preserved for study.
By Easter 1972 hundreds of people were flocking to the house, and various faces appeared over more than thirty years.
A 1993 analysis by Luis Ruiz-Noguez found zinc, lead and chromium cations in the floor, indicating the use of paint.
Infrared photography showed added pigmentation over the original appearance with paintbrush bristles perceptible, and skeptical researchers suspect the faces were made for financial gain.

segments.narration: A face appeared in a woman's kitchen floor overnight. The 23rd of August, 1971. Belmez de la Moraleda, in Jaen, southern Spain.
Maria Gomez Camara called her family in. They destroyed the image. A second face formed. This time the mayor ordered it preserved for study.
By Easter 1972 hundreds of people were queuing at the house. Over thirty years more faces came and went. Nobody ever caught one in the act of appearing.
Then the laboratory answered it. Analysis of the floor turned up zinc, lead and chromium — the chemical signature of paint pigments.
Infrared photography finished the job: pigment added over the original marks, with the bristle strokes of a paintbrush still visible inside them.

research.summary: The Belmez Faces began on 23 August 1971 at Calle Real 5 in Belmez de la Moraleda, Jaen. Faces recurred for over thirty years and drew hundreds of visitors from Easter 1972. The debunking evidence is chemical and photographic: Luis Ruiz-Noguez's 1993 analysis found zinc, lead and chromium indicating paint, and infrared photography showed added pigmentation with visible paintbrush bristles. A 2014 forensic analysis reportedly disagreed, but its own investigator described his conclusion as bewilderment, so the narration rests on the pigment and infrared evidence and does not claim the case is universally closed.

verification.note: Confirmed, at Calle Real 5.

verification.note: Confirmed verbatim.

verification.claim: Infrared showed added pigmentation and paintbrush bristles; a hoax for financial gain is suspected.

stories.description: A Swedish wreck-hunting team's 2011 sonar sweep of the Gulf of Bothnia produced an image the tabloids called a crashed saucer. Geologists who looked at the actual samples found something far older. #unsolvedmysteries #history #baltic
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's strongest hooks pin an impossible object to a real place with a number (Bloop, 133.1%; SS Huronian, 107.2%), so this hook leads on the sonar image and its size and leaves the year and the sea to line two.

factual_claims.text: The Baltic Sea anomaly is a formation roughly 60 metres, about 200 feet, across, found by sonar in June 2011 in the Gulf of Bothnia between Sweden and Finland.
The Swedish OceanX team of Peter Lindberg and Dennis Asberg suggested the feature had unusual characteristics of seemingly non-natural origin, prompting UFO speculation in tabloids.
The team reported structural features and a runway-like track, and retrieved samples from the site.
Volker Bruchert of Stockholm University identified the samples as granites, gneisses and sandstones, consistent with a natural glacial deposit.

Finnish geomorphologist Jarmo Korteniemi identified the runway feature as a natural drumlin, and Hanumant Singh of Woods Hole called the sonar image virtually useless because the equipment was cheap and improperly calibrated.

segments.narration: A sonar scan showed a 200-foot disc on the seabed. June 2011. The Gulf of Bothnia, in the northern Baltic, between Sweden and Finland.
The Swedish team hunting wrecks — Peter Lindberg and Dennis Asberg — said it had features of seemingly non-natural origin. The tabloids printed crashed saucer.
They reported right angles. A track running up to it like a runway. And then they brought pieces of it back up. So what was actually down there?
Rock. Volker Bruchert at Stockholm University identified the samples as granite, gneiss and sandstone — ordinary stone, dropped here by ice age glaciers.
A Finnish geomorphologist read the runway as a natural drumlin. And Woods Hole called the famous sonar image virtually useless: cheap gear, badly calibrated.

research.summary: The Baltic Sea anomaly was found by the Swedish OceanX team (Peter Lindberg, Dennis Asberg) by sonar in June 2011 in the Gulf of Bothnia; it is about 60 m across. Geological analysis by Volker Bruchert of Stockholm University identified granites, gneisses and sandstones consistent with a glacial deposit or rock outcrop, Jarmo Korteniemi read the runway feature as a drumlin, and Hanumant Singh of Woods Hole dismissed the sonar image as virtually useless. The depth is not asserted because the consulted source did not state it.

stories.title: Los Angeles Fired 1,400 Shells At An Empty Sky In 1942
stories.description: For an hour in February 1942 the guns defending Los Angeles fired on an enemy that was never there. Five people died, no bombs fell, and the official answer took forty-one years. #history #unsolvedmysteries #worldwarii
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's evidence favours an exact number in the opening line (Anglo-Zanzibar War's 9:02-9:40; Wow signal's 72 seconds) over scene-setting openers, so this hook leads on the shell count and the emptiness and holds the date for line two.

hook_candidates.text: Los Angeles fired 1,400 shells at an empty sky
hook_candidates.why: A number and a contradiction in nine words, instantly legible.

hook_candidates.text: Five people died in a battle with no enemy
hook_candidates.why: Strong paradox, slightly less specific than the shell count.

hook_candidates.text: For an hour a US city shot at nothing
hook_candidates.why: Vaguest of the three where the brief rewards precision.

hook_choice.reason: The shell count is checkable and the phrase 'empty sky' opens the only loop that matters: what were they shooting at?

factual_claims.text: On 25 February 1942 anti-aircraft batteries over Los Angeles fired more than 1,400 shells, with sirens sounding at 2:25 am and artillery fire beginning at 3:16 am.
Gunners reported aircraft and initially claimed four planes shot down, but no enemy aircraft were confirmed present and none were shot down.
No bombs were dropped and five civilians died, three in blackout car crashes and two of heart attacks.
Navy Secretary Frank Knox held a press conference calling the incident a false alarm caused by anxiety and war nerves.
In 1983 the US Office of Air Force History concluded that a meteorological balloon triggered the alarm and that searchlights and shell bursts created imaginary targets in the sky.

segments.narration: Los Angeles fired 1,400 shells at an empty sky. The 25th of February, 1942. Sirens at 2:25 in the morning. The guns opened up at 3:16.
Searchlights swept the coast. Batteries fired for roughly an hour. Gunners reported aircraft overhead, and four of them shot down. Nothing ever fell.
No bombs. No wreckage. Five people died — three in blackout car crashes, two of heart attacks. So who exactly were they shooting at?
Navy Secretary Frank Knox called it a false alarm the next day. War nerves. Nobody believed him, and the papers ran cover-up theories for decades.
In 1983 the Air Force put it on the record. A stray weather balloon started it — then searchlights and shell bursts manufactured targets out of smoke.

research.summary: The Great Los Angeles Air Raid of 24-25 February 1942 saw over 1,400 anti-aircraft shells fired by the 37th Coast Artillery Brigade at targets that did not exist. No bombs fell, no aircraft were downed, and five civilians died indirectly. Frank Knox called it a false alarm from war nerves at the time; the US Office of Air Force History concluded in 1983 that a lost weather balloon triggered it, compounded by searchlights and shell bursts. Japan confirmed after the war that it flew no aircraft over the area.

verification.note: Confirmed by both sources; the shell count and the 1983 conclusion were independently corroborated in reporting on the incident.

verification.note: Confirmed: no bombs dropped, no enemy aircraft confirmed, zero planes downed.

stories.title: Two Italian Cities Fought A War Named For One Bucket
stories.description: A wooden bucket in a Modena tower gave its name to a 1325 war between Bologna and Modena — but it never started anything. The real trigger was a castle, and the bucket was the souvenir. #history #bizarrehistory #medieval
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief shows that the hooks holding attention state something absurd but literally true (Anglo-Zanzibar War, a war measured in minutes), so this hook claims only what is verifiable — that the war is named for a bucket — rather than repeating the myth that the bucket caused it.

hook_candidates.text: A medieval war is named after a stolen wooden bucket
hook_candidates.why: Absurd and strictly true, since the misnaming is the story.

hook_candidates.text: Thirty-two thousand troops lost to seven thousand in 1325
hook_candidates.why: Great number, but fronts the date and needs sides named.

factual_claims.text: The 1325 conflict between Bologna and Modena in northern Italy is known as the War of the Bucket.
The war's only battle was the Battle of Zappolino, where Bologna fielded 32,000 troops against Modena's roughly 7,000 under Passerino Bonacolsi, and the Bolognese were routed.
The popular account that the war began when a bucket was stolen from a well is largely incorrect.
The war was triggered by Modena's capture of the Bolognese castle of Monteveglio, within the Guelph-Ghibelline conflict between papal and imperial supporters that ran over 300 years.
The bucket was taken as a trophy by the Modenese after the war and is kept at the Torre della Ghirlandina in Modena.

segments.narration: A medieval war is named after a stolen wooden bucket. 1325. Bologna against Modena, in northern Italy.
One battle settled it, at Zappolino. Bologna marched 32,000 men. Modena had about 7,000 under Passerino Bonacolsi. Bologna was routed.
The bucket is the part everyone remembers. Snatched from a city well, the story goes, and a war followed. Except that is not what happened.
The real trigger was territory: Modena had seized the Bolognese castle of Monteveglio. Under that sat the Guelph and Ghibelline feud — pope's side against emperor's, running three centuries.
And the bucket? A trophy, taken after the fighting. It still hangs in Modena's Ghirlandina tower: a souvenir that stole the credit for an entire war.

research.summary: The War of the Bucket (1325) between Bologna and Modena was decided at the Battle of Zappolino, where Bologna's 32,000 troops were routed by Modena's roughly 7,000 under Passerino Bonacolsi. The bucket did not cause the war: Modena's capture of the Bolognese castle of Monteveglio was the trigger, within the wider Guelph-Ghibelline conflict, and the bucket was taken as a post-battle trophy now kept at the Torre della Ghirlandina. Casualty detail is kept non-graphic.

verification.note: Confirmed. The hook deliberately claims only the naming, not the cause.

verification.note: Confirmed, with the source attributing the trophy account to one source; the narration follows it as the corrected version.

stories.title: Divers Found A Stone Road Under The Bahamas In 1968
stories.description: Half a mile of rectangular blocks lies eighteen feet down off North Bimini, and it looks unmistakably laid by hand. The rock itself explains how it got there. #unsolvedmysteries #history #archaeology
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's strong hooks lead on a physical impossibility a viewer can picture (Mirage of Constanz, 187.7%), so this hook leads on the line of blocks underwater and holds the year, depth and location for line two.

hook_candidates.text: Divers found a half-mile line of stone blocks underwater
hook_candidates.why: Instantly visual, and the loop is who put them there.

hook_candidates.text: These underwater blocks look laid by hand. Nothing laid them
hook_candidates.why: Resolves the mystery inside the hook itself.

hook_candidates.text: A lost civilisation was announced off the Bahamas in 1968
hook_candidates.why: Fronts the claim and the date rather than the object.

factual_claims.text: The Bimini Road was discovered on 2 September 1968 by Joseph Manson Valentine and colleagues, lies about 5.5 metres or 18 feet underwater off North Bimini in the Bahamas, and runs about 0.8 km.
The formation is made of roughly rectangular limestone blocks averaging two to three metres, the largest three to four metres, with highly rounded corners likened to giant loaves of bread.
Claims about the formation have included a lost civilisation and Atlantis, and Gavin Menzies falsely claimed the Chinese admiral Zheng He built it around 1421.
Geologists and archaeologists concluded the formation is natural beachrock, carbonate-cemented shell hash native to the Bahamas, broken into blocks along orthogonal and other natural joints.

Radiocarbon dating places the shells at about 3,500 years old, erosion exposed the beachrock roughly 1,900 to 2,000 years ago, and similar natural tessellated pavements occur off Tasmania and in Utah.

segments.narration: Divers found a half-mile line of stone blocks underwater. September 1968. Eighteen feet down, off North Bimini in the Bahamas.
Roughly rectangular blocks, two to four metres across, corners worn perfectly round. Laid out in one straight line, like giant loaves of bread.
The claims came fast. A lost civilisation. Atlantis. Even a story that a Chinese admiral built it in 1421. So who cut these stones?
Nobody. It is beachrock — shell and sand cemented into limestone, native to the Bahamas, which cracks along straight natural joints as it breaks up.
Radiocarbon puts the shells near 3,500 years old, and the sea uncovered them roughly 2,000 years ago. The same pavements form off Tasmania and in Utah.

research.summary: The Bimini Road, found 2 September 1968 off North Bimini, is a 0.8 km line of rounded rectangular beachrock blocks in about 5.5 m of water. Geologists and archaeologists including Shinn, McKusick, Gifford, Ball, Davaud and Strasser conclude it formed naturally: beachrock cemented below the surface, exposed by coastal erosion roughly 1,900-2,000 years ago, and fractured along orthogonal joints. Shells date to c.3,500 years. Comparable natural tessellated pavements occur in Tasmania, Utah and off Florida. The Edgar Cayce 1968 prophecy detail was left out because the consulted source did not confirm it.

verification.note: All confirmed.

verification.claim: Natural beachrock, carbonate-cemented shell hash, fractured along orthogonal joints.
verification.note: Confirmed as the scientific consensus.

stories.title: Greece's Most Famous Oracle Sat Above A Gas Vent
stories.description: For over a thousand years kings consulted a priestess who prophesied in a trance at Delphi, and ancient writers blamed vapours from the rock. Geologists found the faults and named the gas. #history #unsolvedmysteries #ancientgreece
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's top hook cohort states a physical fact that reframes a familiar subject (Bloop, 133.1%), so this hook puts the temple on top of leaking faults in the first line instead of easing in through Delphi's fame.

hook_candidates.text: The oracle's temple sat on two faults leaking sweet gas
hook_candidates.why: Reframes a famous subject with a physical fact in one line.

hook_candidates.text: A priestess prophesied for a thousand years above a crack
hook_candidates.why: Atmospheric but vaguer, and 'crack' undersells it.

hook_candidates.text: Ancient writers said vapours rose under her. They were right
hook_candidates.why: Needs a referent for 'her' before it lands.

hook_choice.reason: It puts the geology and the prophecy in the same breath, which is the whole story, and needs no knowledge of Delphi to sound wrong.

factual_claims.text: The Temple of Apollo at Delphi in central Greece housed the oracle from at least the 8th century BC until about AD 390.
The Pythia delivered prophecies from a gilded tripod in the temple's inner sanctum, the adyton, while in a trance state, with priests recasting her words into verse.
Ancient sources, particularly Plutarch, described intoxicating vapours rising from an underground fissure beneath the temple floor.

In the 1980s geologist Jelle Zeilinga de Boer, archaeologist John Hale, chemist Jeffrey Chanton and toxicologist Henry Spiller found that the Kerna and Delphic fault lines cross directly below where the adyton stood.

The team proposed ethylene, a sweet-smelling gas from bituminous limestone that produces euphoria in small doses, while critics including Daryn Lehoux have disputed whether the concentrations were sufficient.

segments.narration: The oracle's temple sat on two faults leaking sweet gas. Delphi, central Greece. Kings and generals came here for over a thousand years.
The Pythia sat on a gilded tripod in the inner sanctum, the adyton. She went into a trance. Priests recast what came out as verse.
Plutarch wrote that intoxicating vapours rose from a fissure under the floor. For centuries that was filed away as temple myth. It was not.
In the 1980s a geologist, an archaeologist, a chemist and a toxicologist mapped the site. Two fault lines, Kerna and Delphic, cross directly beneath the sanctum.
Below them: bituminous limestone. The gas is ethylene — sweet-smelling, and in small doses euphoric. Critics still argue the dose. The faults are not in doubt.

research.summary: The Delphic oracle operated at the Temple of Apollo from at least the 8th century BC until c.AD 390. A four-year interdisciplinary study by de Boer (geology), Hale (archaeology), Chanton (chemistry) and Spiller (toxicology) identified the Kerna and Delphic faults crossing beneath the adyton over bituminous limestone, and found ethane, methane and ethylene in nearby spring water (ethylene at 0.3 ppm today, likely higher in antiquity). Ethylene causes euphoria and a floating sensation in small doses. The hypothesis is contested — Daryn Lehoux argued it is impossible, and methane and CO2/H2S have been proposed instead — so the narration states the faults as established and the dose as disputed.

stories.title: He Filmed The First Movie, Then Vanished From A Train
stories.description: Louis Le Prince shot moving pictures in Leeds in 1888, years before Edison's public claim. In 1890 he boarded a train at Dijon and was never seen again — no body, no luggage. #unsolvedmysteries #history #cinema
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's strongest hooks state a vanishing plainly and specifically (Flight 19, 112.1%, 'fourteen men walked into the Florida sky and never returned'), so this hook pairs the achievement and the disappearance in one line before any name or date.

hook_candidates.text: He shot the first moving picture, then vanished off a train
hook_candidates.why: Achievement and vanishing collide in one line, the Flight 19 shape.

hook_candidates.text: Cinema's real inventor disappeared weeks before he could prove it
hook_candidates.why: Strong, but 'real inventor' asks the viewer to take a side first.

hook_candidates.text: A man boarded at Dijon and never got off
hook_candidates.why: Good loop, but without the achievement it is just a missing person.

hook_choice.reason: The collision is the story: the man who did it first is also the man who disappeared, and both halves land in eleven words.

factual_claims.text: Louis Le Prince filmed Roundhay Garden Scene in Leeds on 14 October 1888 using his single-lens camera.
Le Prince vanished on 16 September 1890 after saying goodbye to his brother at Dijon and boarding a train for Paris, and never arrived.
Neither Le Prince's body nor his luggage was ever recovered, and a public exhibition of his films was planned at the Morris-Jumel Mansion in Manhattan for September 1890.
Theories for his disappearance include suicide over financial difficulties, murder linked to the motion-picture patent disputes involving Edison, and a voluntary disappearance.
A photograph of a drowned man resembling Le Prince was found in Paris police archives, and Le Prince was declared dead in absentia on 16 September 1897.

segments.narration: He shot the first moving picture, then vanished off a train. Louis Le Prince. October 1888, Leeds — seconds of his family walking in a garden.
The 16th of September, 1890. He says goodbye to his brother at Dijon and boards the express for Paris. He never gets off it.
No body. No luggage. Nothing recovered, then or since. And a public showing of his films was already booked in Manhattan.
The theories piled up. Suicide over money. Murder over the patents, with Edison's camp the suspect. A family quarrel. A simple robbery.
A photograph of a drowned man resembling him later surfaced in Paris police files. It is the closest anyone has come. He was declared dead in absentia in 1897.

Theories include suicide over money, murder tied to the patent disputes involving Edison, and voluntary disappearance; none is conclusive. A photograph of a drowning victim resembling him was found in Paris police archives. He was declared dead in absentia in 1897. It spread. Ninety-five of the school's one hundred fifty-nine pupils were affected, in fits that ran from hours to sixteen days.

The school closed in March. The laughter went home with the girls, reached Nshamba village, and eventually touched about a thousand people across fourteen schools.

The school closed on 18 March 1962; the outbreak spread to Nshamba and other communities within about a 100-mile radius of Bukoba, closing 14 schools and affecting roughly 1,000 people over some 18 months. Medical officers A. M. Rankin and P. J. Philip investigated and published in the Central African Journal of Medicine in 1963, concluding it was mass psychogenic illness — real symptoms with no infectious or toxic cause, later analysed by Bartholomew, Wessely and Hempelmann as conversion reactions under cultural and academic stress in a newly independent country.

segments.narration: A sheet of paper won't fit between these hundred-ton stones. Sacsayhuamán, above Cusco, at three thousand seven hundred metres.
No mortar. Every block a different shape, and every one meets its neighbours exactly. Three terraced walls, each about four hundred metres long.
The limestone came from quarries kilometres away, over Andean ridges, with no iron tools, no wheels and no draft animals. So how?
Cieza de León wrote in fifteen fifty-three that Pachacuti put twenty thousand men on it, four thousand quarrying, six thousand hauling on leather cables.

Best reconstruction: pounded to shape with hammerstones, hauled on ropes and ramps, test-fitted again and again. And the crooked joints are the point. Inca walls settle back into place when the ground shakes.

research.summary: Sacsayhuamán is an Inca walled complex on the northern edge of Cusco, Peru, at 3,701 m. Its three main terrace walls run about 400 m and are built of limestone blocks of roughly 128 to nearly 200 tonnes, fitted without mortar; Pedro Cieza de León wrote in 1553 that 'a rial could not be put in between two of them' and that Pachacuti set 20,000 workers on the site, 4,000 quarrying and 6,000 hauling with leather cables. After the conquest the finer masonry was quarried for colonial Cusco, leaving the largest blocks. Wikipedia's Inca architecture article records that stones were initially fitted using hammerstones, whose impact marks survive on many faces, that blocks were lifted with rope slings and adjusted by eye, and that inclined walls with rounded corners and thorough masonry gave Inca buildings 'peerless seismic resistance', with blocks observed settling back into position after strong earthquakes.

segments.narration: A New York paper reported bat-winged people living on the moon. The Sun ran it as news in August eighteen thirty-five.
Six articles. Lunar bison, goats with a single horn, beaches, temples, and Vespertilio-homo, man-bats who walked upright and flew.
It was all credited to Sir John Herschel, a real astronomer, genuinely observing at the Cape of Good Hope. He knew nothing about it.
New York believed it. A committee of Yale scientists came down to read the original journal articles. There were none. Who writes this, and why?
Richard Adams Locke, a Sun reporter, wrote it as satire of serious claims that the moon was populated. The Sun admitted the fabrication on the sixteenth of September and never printed a retraction.

research.summary: The Great Moon Hoax was a series of six articles in the New York Sun beginning 25 August 1835, purporting to report Sir John Herschel's discovery of life on the moon through a vast new telescope at the Cape of Good Hope. The articles described lunar bison, single-horned goats, tail-less beavers, beaches and temples, and winged humanoids named Vespertilio-homo, or man-bats. They were attributed to Herschel via a fictitious companion, Dr Andrew Grant; Herschel, who really was observing at the Cape, had nothing to do with them. Readers took them as fact, and a committee of Yale scientists travelled to New York looking for the non-existent Edinburgh Journal of Science originals. Sun reporter Richard Adams Locke, who publicly admitted authorship in 1840, is accepted as the author and is understood to have written the pieces as satire of contemporary speculation about extraterrestrial life. The Sun acknowledged the articles were fabricated on 16 September 1835 but issued no formal retraction.

The jars range from about 1 to 3 metres in height and weigh up to about six tonnes, carved from stone.

segments.narration: A field of giant stone jars nobody could safely excavate. More than two thousand of them, across the Xiangkhoang Plateau in Laos.
Up to three metres tall, six tonnes each, carved from solid rock. Nobody living remembers putting them there.
And archaeologists mostly couldn't get near them. Around two hundred and seventy million cluster bombs were dropped on this plateau. Roughly eighty million never went off.
Clearance work from two thousand four opened the sites. Optical dating put the jars in place as early as around twelve forty BC.
Inside and around them: human bone, beads, iron tools. They are funerary vessels, a plateau-sized graveyard, and what kept it a mystery was a war three thousand years too late.

research.summary: The Plain of Jars is a megalithic landscape on the Xiangkhoang Plateau in Laos, with more than 2,100 carved stone jars recorded across more than 120 sites. The jars stand roughly 1 to 3 metres tall and weigh up to about six tonnes, with the largest site holding several hundred. Optically stimulated luminescence dating places jars in position as early as 1240 to 660 BC, and excavations from Madeleine Colani onward have recovered human remains, glass beads, spindle whorls and bronze and iron tools, supporting the accepted reading of the jars as Iron Age funerary vessels used for secondary burial. An estimated 270 million cluster bombs were dropped or dumped on the plateau, of which around 80 million failed to detonate, which severely restricted archaeological access until clearance operations began in 2004. UNESCO inscribed the Megalithic Jar Sites in Xiengkhuang on the World Heritage List in 2019.

segments.narration: Henry Ford built an American town in the Amazon rainforest. Nineteen twenty-eight, on the Tapajos River in Brazil. He called it Fordlandia.
About two and a half million acres, all for rubber. Clapboard houses, a water tower, hamburgers, square dances, and no alcohol.
Workers rioted in nineteen thirty over the canteen food. But the thing that actually killed Fordlandia was not the people.
Rubber trees grow wild and scattered in the Amazon for a reason. Planted in tight rows, they hand South American leaf blight one continuous meal.
The blight took it. Belterra, downstream, died the same way. In nineteen forty-five Ford's grandson sold both back to Brazil at a loss above twenty million dollars, and Henry Ford never once visited.

research.summary: Fordlandia was founded in 1928 by Henry Ford on the east bank of the Tapajos River, about 300 km south of Santarem in Para, Brazil, on a concession of roughly 2.5 million acres, as a rubber plantation and prefabricated American-style town intended for 10,000 residents. American housing, diet and social rules, including prohibition of alcohol, provoked the 1930 'Breaking Pans' (Quebra-Panelas) revolt. The plantation failed biologically: Hevea rubber planted densely in its native range is highly vulnerable to South American leaf blight, along with ants, lace bugs and caterpillars, in a way that scattered wild trees and the transplanted Asian plantations were not. Fordlandia was abandoned in 1934 and operations moved downstream to Belterra, which also failed. In 1945 Henry Ford II sold both sites back to Brazil at a loss exceeding $20 million. Henry Ford never visited either site; most of the original structures still stand and the area had around 3,000 residents as of 2017.

verification.note: Wikipedia records the 1930 Quebra-Panelas ('Breaking Pans') revolt over imposed dietary restrictions and food distribution changes.

verification.claim: Densely planted rubber trees in the Amazon are devastated by South American leaf blight, which does not spread the same way through scattered wild trees.
verification.note: Wikipedia attributes the failure to blight plus ants, lace bugs, red spiders and caterpillars in dense plantations; the contrast with naturally scattered Hevea and with blight-free Asian plantations is the standard account and is given in the Damn Interesting piece.

verification.claim: Fordlandia was abandoned in 1934 and its Belterra replacement also failed; in 1945 Henry Ford II sold both back to Brazil at a loss of over $20 million, and Henry Ford never visited.
verification.note: Wikipedia: abandoned 1934, operations moved to Belterra, and in 1945 Henry Ford II sold both sites back to Brazil for a loss exceeding $20 million; Ford's never having visited is recorded in both sources.
